score_meanings.promise_vocabulary: 0 drifts into claims/profiles/central trust-ledger framing, 5 stays promise-first and pCID-specific
score_meanings.simplicity_durability: 0 overbuilt or fragile, 5 minimal, durable, and small-device-friendly under the 100-year goal

promise_theory_rules: A promise is a scoped declaration of intent.
No agent can make a promise on behalf of another agent.
Trust is a local assessment of whether a promise will be kept.
Promises to receive or use are not equivalent to obligations, impositions, or promises to give.
promise_theory_references: Mark Burgess, In Search of Certainty
Mark Burgess, Promise Theory: Principles and Applications

assessment.rationale: Strong local audit evidence shapes and good plane separation, but weak direct fit for transferable promise-token pressure. It helps provenance and refusal auditability, yet does not define transfer, spend, or re-acceptance semantics well enough. Useful design material, but it needs a promise-first reframe.
strengths: Exact audit-anchor citation improves later provenance checks.
Clear live/audit/storage/device separation reduces hash-equals-authorization confusion.
Peer-local append-only records support sparse-knowledge audit.
Break-witness default is strong for ambiguous non-idempotent effects.
weaknesses: Does not specify transferable token lifecycle, spend rules, or refusal flow.
Uses claim-card vocabulary instead of explicit promise payload wording.
Authoritative-boundary/shared-family framing can sound more centralized than local trust assessment.
risks: Carol may overread a transferred artifact as a direct Alice promise to her.
Double-spend prevention may drift toward central-ledger logic because no local transfer protocol is defined.
Claim-card vocabulary may invite normative conformance reading instead of local trust assessment.
open_questions: How should Alice express transferability or non-transferability without implying a promise to Carol on Bob's behalf?
What local record pattern would show spend, revocation, or refusal without introducing global uniqueness authority?
Can audit-anchor chains carry delegation/provenance for transferred artifacts without turning claim cards into obligation tokens?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.

autonomous_agents.note: Peers publish their own scoped artifacts and keep local records; no single global actor is required.

scoped_intent.note: Scope planes and exact audit anchors bound intent clearly, though the wording is claim-centric rather than promise-first.

no_promises_for_others.note: Mostly respected, but shared app-family and authoritative-boundary framing can blur which agent is actually making which promise.

no_guaranteed_outcomes.note: Hashes and audit anchors do not guarantee availability, retention, or effect completion; break-witness handling reinforces this.

local_trust_assessment.note: Trust remains local through cited immutable anchors and peer-local append-only records.

accept_use_not_obligation.note: The design avoids equating possession of a hash or card with authorization, but transferable-token acceptance/refusal semantics are not fully modeled.

violations: The design centers scoped claim cards and authoritative-boundary claims instead of direct scoped agent promises.
Transferable-token semantics are underspecified, so Bob's transfer risks being misread as Alice promising Carol something.
